content: Ampicillin injection is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating various infections, including respiratory tract infections, bacterial infections, septicemia, endocarditis, urinary tract infections, and gastrointestinal infections. It is a broad-spectrum beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, leading to bacterial death. Ampicillin is effective against many Gram-positive and some Gram-negative bacteria, including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and Neisseria meningitidis. However, it is not resistant to destruction by beta-lactamase enzymes. The drug is available as a sterile sodium salt for intramuscular or intravenous use, with dosages tailored to the type and severity of the infection. For adults, typical dosages range from 250 mg to 2 g every 6 hours, depending on the infection. Pediatric dosages are calculated based on body weight, typically 150-200 mg/kg/day, divided into doses every 3-4 hours. Ampicillin therapy should continue for at least 48-72 hours after symptoms resolve or bacterial eradication is confirmed. For Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections, a minimum of 10 days of treatment is recommended to prevent complications like acute rheumatic fever. Ampicillin is generally well-tolerated, but adverse reactions can occur. Common side effects include gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and pseudomembranous colitis. Hypersensitivity reactions, including skin rashes, urticaria, and anaphylaxis, have been reported, particularly in individuals with a history of penicillin allergy. Serious anaphylactic reactions require immediate emergency treatment with epinephrine, oxygen, and intravenous steroids. Hematologic reactions, such as anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia, are rare and usually reversible upon discontinuation of therapy. Ampicillin is excreted largely unchanged in the urine, and its excretion can be delayed by concurrent administration of probenecid. It penetrates most body tissues and fluids but achieves therapeutic levels in the cerebrospinal fluid only when the meninges are inflamed. The drug is minimally protein-bound, with approximately 20% binding compared to 60-90% for other penicillins. Ampicillin is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA, indicating no evidence of harm to the fetus in animal studies, but adequate human studies are lacking. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use during labor, delivery, or in nursing mothers. Similarly, there is limited information on its use in geriatric, pediatric, or immunocompromised populations, as well as in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. In cases of overdose, ampicillin should be discontinued, and symptomatic and supportive measures should be instituted. Hemodialysis can remove ampicillin-class antibiotics in patients with impaired renal function, but peritoneal dialysis is ineffective. Ampicillin should be stored at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F). The vials do not contain natural rubber latex. There is no established interaction between alcohol and ampicillin, but patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding alcohol consumption while on this medication.
